items.title: It's not clear when iPhone 18 Pro and folding iPhone preorders will start
items.content_html:
Apple will reportedly sidestep a September 11 preorder date by moving sales to Saturday, only to burden buyers with a significantly less convenient start time.

Typically Apple holds its yearly iPhone launch on or around the second Tuesday. This hasn't always been the case; out of the last eight iPhone events, we've had five Tuesdays, two Wednesdays, and one Monday.

And, in 2020, that launch was in October, not September. So it's not a hard and fast rule.

This year, we're getting our September Apple Event on Wednesday, September 9. Apple is expected to announce the iPhone 18 Pro and its first foldable phone, the iPhone Ultra.

Historically, Apple almost always opens preorders the following Friday. But there is one exception to that rule: when the following Friday falls on September 11.

In 2015, Apple announced the iPhone 6s and iPhone 6s Plus on Wednesday, September 9. Preorders subsequently fell on Saturday, September 12.

It looks like Apple is going to repeat that pattern this year. According to Macwelt's sources, Apple plans to follow the this year's iPhone event by opening preorders on Saturday.

There may be one significant change, though. Instead of opening Preorders at 5:00 am PT or 8:00 am ET, the company will allegedly be opening preorders at 12:01 am PT, as it has done for iPhones in the past.

This means that anyone on the east coast will need to preorder at 3:01am ET.

If true, this would be wildly inconvenient to most of the U.S. While one could argue that 5:00 am is not a convenient time to wake up to place a preorder, it's still not unheard of.

Expecting someone in Chicago, for example, to either stay up or set an alarm for 2:00 am seems a bit cruel. Especially considering Apple will be launching the iPhone Ultra, a phone that will most assuredly have very limited supplies to begin with.

AppleInsider has also spoken with sources at a major U.S. carrier who have been told to keep the morning of September 11 open, with time-off requests for that period being denied.

However, that doesn't necessarily mean preorders will begin Friday morning. We were also told that the carrier has been wrong in the past, leaving stores to adjust their plans once Apple announced the concrete date.

We won't know officially until Apple announces preorders at the September Apple Event. You can use our helpful guide for when and where to tune in to see it live.

items.title: Apple's latest price hike is to Apple TV streaming and Apple One
items.content_html:
Apple's latest round of price increases isn't for hardware, but for Apple TV video streaming and, correspondingly, some Apple One tiers.

Announced on Friday, Apple TV's monthly cost is increasing by $2 to $14.99 per month. This raises the annual cost to $119, up from $99.

This affects some Apple One subscriptions as well. While the family plan monthly cost isn't going up, the individual plan is.

Effective at your next billing cycle, if you're an Apple One individual subscriber, you're going to get billed $21.95 instead of $19.95. It does not appear at this time that Apple One Premier is impacted.

In July, Apple hiked Apple Music pricing to $11.99 per month, with the family plan climbing to $19.99 per month.

Then, the Apple One family and Premier tiers increased in cost to $27.95 and $39.95, respectively.

Video streaming competitors are in the ballpark. Disney+ with Hulu costs $19.99 per month or $189.99 per year for an ad-free experience. Netflix costs $19.99 per month for HD, and $26.99 per month for 4K with HDR and Dolby Atmos for four devices.

Both Netflix and Disney+ have more content than Apple TV does.

items.title: PSA: Don't use a free iPhone that just turns up at your home
items.content_html:
If you get an unexpected iPhone shipped to you using it is just giving hackers your bank accounts and passwords. Here's what to look for, who to tell about it, and how to deal with it.

Well, maybe you do have a secret admirer, we're not judging and you are looking very good today. But a surprise gift of an iPhone will seem to be too good to be true because it is.

It will have been sent to you, or someone in your life who has a big job, in the hope, and possibly the fair expectation, that you won't question your luck and instead will enjoy the phone. Then every single thing you do on that phone is harvested and sent to fraudsters.

Passwords are the obvious first issue. If you log into this device, and use it, you are giving them those plus account details and verification codes.

But then through that, you're giving them enough to impersonate you.

How it happens and what to look for

What to look for couldn't be easier. If it's an iPhone you didn't order and which your spouse or IT department looks blank about when you thank them for it, that's enough.

As for how it happens, a Reddit user has recounted what just happened to them. Showing a photo of a sealed iPhone 15 Pro Max, they say it "showed up at our house even though we never ordered it."

"Things got weirder when I checked it," they continue. "The serial number on the iPhone box is recognized by Apple as an iPhone 15 Pro Max. Apple says that the serial number was purchased/activated in December 2023 and its coverage expired in 2024."

Remember, the box was sealed. It also came with a FedEx shipping label, but the Reddit user says its number wasn't found when they searched FedEx's online tracker.

We have some questions about the authenticity of the account, but the lesson to be taught here is a good one.

How much this is worth to attackers

If you ever doubt that it's financially worth it to cyber attack someone, examine what happened here. True, it's unlikely that the hacker bought the iPhone, although if they did, that model retailed from $1,200 back in 2023.

What's much more likely is that the phone was stolen, but then the thief would be bound to get some cash from simply selling it, even if just for parts. Sending it to you unsolicited and for free sounds like throwing money away.

It is in this case. That Reddit user is not going to turn on that iPhone so this was a waste of the hacker's time and money.

But just as you know that ridiculously obvious spam emails keep coming because enough people are fooled, these bad actors are playing the percentages. Enough people will turn on and use these free iPhones that it is worth sending them out.

It's a decent chance that just one person using one of these iPhones is enough, too. Just one person could be enough because these bad actors could gain everything they need to totally clear out someone's life savings.

Whale phishing

As this kind of cyberattack is targeted at one individual at a time. It's about getting access to their accounts, and its become known as another form of Whale Phishing.

That used to be solely the name for a really targeted cyberattack against one individual in a corporation. It would be against someone like the CEO, whom no one would question if they ordered millions of dollars to be transferred around.

You may not handle millions of dollars, but every dollar is yours and it wouldn't just be at risk, it would be gone. So the absolutely mandatory way to protect yourself is to never use an iPhone whose provenance you don't know.

And, if you're associated with a big company, you should probably tell your IT department about it. They may want to see it, and they may not. Do not let them just shrug about it, though.

After that, you could take it to an Apple Store to be recycled or you could throw it in any other ewaste recycling bin. Presumably, it still has a lithium ion battery so don't just toss it in the trash.

Either disposal option is better than turning the thing on and using it.

items.title: If you're going to the iPhone 18 Pro event, there's a 'Welcome Run'
items.content_html:
Attendees to the September 9 iPhone 18 Pro event are being invited to warm up the night before, with a fun walk, run, or wheelchair lap at Apple Park.

Apple has just confirmed that its September special event titled "Surprise and shine" will be taking place on September 9. However, for those who turn up the night before, they get to take part in another activity.

Attendees to the Wednesday event are being invited to take part in a "Welcome Run, Walk, or Roll" on the evening of September 8. Hosted by the Apple Fitness+ team, the registration explains that it will take place around the Apple Park Ring.

The event will take place at 5 P.M. Pacific time and last for an hour. Participants can choose their pace and distance, up to three laps around the ring or 3 miles.

It is typical for those attending Apple's major events to arrive at least the day before so they can make an early start for the next day's festivities. A small event the evening before a major event is unusual, but could serve to be a good brand activation exercise for Apple.

And, a good networking opportunity for the attendees.

While it may be the case that Apple has something fitness-related or a new Apple Watch for the September 9 show itself, it's unlikely Apple will spoil that in a pre-event preview like this.

items.title: World's best selling smartphone is the iPhone 17 - again
items.content_html:
Figures for the second quarter of 2026 show that the iPhone 17 is once more the biggest selling smartphone around the globe, and that Apple takes the next two spots as well.

According to previous figures from Counterpoint Research, the iPhone 17 was the best-selling smartphone in Q1 2026. But that was predicted, since in the months after launch, the trend in iPhone sales is to see an increase in the non-Pro models.

Now the research firm says that the iPhone 17 has continued to be as successful. For Q2 2026, it again took the lead in a top ten of smartphone models by sales.

"Apple's unit sales grew 5% YoY despite a broader market decline," said Senior Analyst Karn Chauhan. "iPhone sales increased across India, Japan, and the MEA, and nearly doubled in South Korea in Q2 2026, driven by the iPhone 17 series."

Counterpoint puts the continued demand for the iPhone 17 down to how it was a significant upgrade on the previous model. Specifically, Apple narrowed the difference between the regular and Pro models with the iPhone 17 range.

Speaking of the range, the number two biggest-selling smartphone in the quarter was the iPhone 17 Pro Max. Third was the iPhone 17 Pro, while the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra came in fourth.

Apple wasn't done with the top ten though, as the iPhone 17e took seventh place. And the iPhone 16 took tenth, meaning that iPhones made up half of the top ten.

This is exactly what happened in the same period in 2025. Apple took first, second, third, seventh, and tenth place, with its iPhone 16 range and the iPhone 15.

For 2026, the global chip shortage has reportedly led to manufacturers concentrating on premium phones. While Apple and Samsung both showed increases, overall the global smartphone market contracted by 11%.

This global pattern of Apple's share going up even as the market goes down, matches recent results from individual territories.

Apple's strong showing in the top ten chart is also reflected in its earnings. Reportedly, despite accounting for 23% of global shipments, Apple captured 49% of worldwide smartphone revenues, according to Counterpoint.

items.title: You can spend $18,299 on a Mac Studio today, or more in October
items.content_html:
Apple is taking pre-orders for the new Mac Studio now, but one configuration can't be selected yet. It's certain to push the maximum price well over $20,000, too.

If you chose to, you could now spend $899 on a base Mac mini and wince at how much more those cost these days. Or you could go the other way and try to max-out a new Mac Studio.

You can try. Very unusually, Apple has opened pre-orders for the Mac Studio but excluded one configuration, which it just says is "coming late October."

That's the configuration of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio with the maximum 512GB of unified memory. That M5 Ultra model starts at 96GB and for now can only be ordered with that or 256GB RAM.

Given that Apple will charge you $4,000 for going up from 96GB RAM to 256GB, the jump to 512GB is not going to be cheap and not just going to be another $4000. Apple does not quote a price yet, either.

What you can get now

It's hard to imagine that a 512GB RAM model will be the biggest seller, but holding it back completely is a sign of the global chip shortage. Nonetheless, it can't be pre-pre-ordered and there will be users who will have no option but to wait.

If you can do with a miserly 256GB RAM, then your maximum configuration available for pre-order consists of:

  • M5 Ultra 36-core CPU, 80-core GPU
  • 256GB unified memory
  • 16TB SSD storage

The base M5 Ultra Mac Studio costs $5,499, and the jump to a 36-core CPU with 80-core GPU adds $1,300. Going from the included 1TB to the maximum 16TB adds $7,500.

As yet you cannot select the promised 512GB RAM configuration of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio - image credit: Apple.

So before any taxes, the current maximum cost of an M5 Ultra Mac Studio is $18,299. You might also want to add AppleCare insurance, but you have to click through the next couple of pages of accessories and services to get there.

That AppleCare box is right on the first page for the MacBook Neo and the iMac, but the same as the Mac Studio, for the new Mac mini.

Apple does list the Mac Studio in its AppleCare One bundle options, though. The current figures say the Mac Studio can be covered under the $19.99 per month base fee.

Remember that you can add AppleCare later, but you cannot upgrade processors, storage, or RAM after ordering. So if you need 512GB RAM, you have to wait before we can find out how much that will cost.

At least Apple doesn't sell wheels for the Mac Studio.

items.title: Incoming Apple CEO John Ternus meets with Tim Cook's friend Pikachu & Pokemon CEO
items.content_html:
The Pokemon team visited Apple Park on their way to the Pokemon World Championship starting on August 28 in San Francisco, giving Pikachu a chance to explore and meet the next CEO of Apple.

One of the perks of being CEO of Apple is meeting all kinds of celebrities. While Tim Cook might be partial to Bono, he's also buddies with a certain electric mouse.

A social media post from Apple CEO Tim Cook revealed Pikachu was set loose in Apple Park. Incoming CEO John Ternus and Pokemon Company CEO Tsunekazu Ishihara helped Tim keep an eye on Pikachu as he explored.

Today's agenda at Apple Park: Introduce the @Pokemon team to John, talk gaming, and politely ask Pikachu to stay out of the pond. Two out of three were accomplished. pic.twitter.com/KzirV3VX8U

— Tim Cook (@tim_cook) August 27, 2026

While the Pokemon Company didn't share why they were at Apple Park, the antics were cute and even showed a scene where Ishinara sent out the Pokemon Applin using the game Pokemon Go. They could be discussing important business surrounding the future of Pokemon on Apple platforms, or simply giving Pikachu a chance to stretch his legs before heading to San Francisco.

The Pokemon Trading Card Game World Championships are being held from August 28-30. While Apple doesn't have a role in that event, it does host several games on the App Store from Nintendo, including Pokemon Go, Pokemon TCG Pocket, Pokemon Champions, and even Pokemon Sleep.

I wouldn't dig into this fun little social media too much. Tim Cook is known for his trips to Japan and has even met Pikachu before while there to celebrate Apple Ginza opening.

items.title: What to expect from Apple's 'Surprise and shine' iPhone 18 Pro event on September 9
items.content_html:
Apple has confirmed its September special event will be held on September 9. It won't just be the iPhone 18 Pro or folding iPhone launch, but also the first event with John Ternus as CEO. Here's what to expect.

Regular as clockwork, Apple holds an event in early September to launch new iPhone models and other products. Apple has just confirmed that this will be the case for 2026's presentation.

Titled "Surprise and shine," the event will be taking place on September 9, starting at 10 A.M. Pacific, 1 P.M. Eastern Time. As usual, it will be streamed on YouTube, the Apple Event page, and the Apple TV app, among other methods.

The event will be the first for the company following the long-awaited CEO transition. John Ternus will take over from Tim Cook on September 1, and will helm the presentation from the outset.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

While there has been some speculation of the return of a live keynote, it's doubtful that Apple will move away from its slick prerecorded video. There will be an on-site event at Apple Park for the media to try out Apple's new launches, if not anything being streamed live.

As always, AppleInsider will be reporting in-depth about the product launches and the event in general.

What to expect for the September event

As with every Apple fall event schedule, there are many products that will launch, but not everything will appear during the prime September showcase. A second and a rare third event can also be held for select products that Apple plans to launch a little later.

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max

The September event is chiefly when Apple launches its update to the iPhone range, and this year it is the iPhone 18 generation. However, it will only be part of the roster due to Apple's decision to split the series into two separate launches.

For September's event, Apple will introduce the premium members of the iPhone 18 family, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

A mock-up of a dark cherry iPhone 18 Pro, one of the rumored colorways.

After the 2025 refresh, the 2026 update is probably going to be a spec-bump update. Chiefly, that will mean a transition to a new 2-nanometer A20 Pro chip, which stands to run cooler for longer thanks to some packaging changes.

You can also count Apple's C2 modem as being included in the model, too. As far as physical changes go, the camera bump may get a little bit bigger and colors like dark cherry may appear, but don't expect a complete overhaul.

When it comes to cameras, there may be a few changes, including the possibility of under-display Face ID. On the back, the iPhone 18 Pro Max may be the only model to gain a variable-aperture camera, which can help create a real bokeh effect instead of a computer-generated version.

What definitely will change is the price. In the wake of the June price rises and the continuing memory crisis, the iPhone 18 Pro could cost $300 more than the iPhone 17 Pro counterparts.

Folding iPhone

The more important iPhone launch for the event will be the iPhone Fold, though it may also be called the iPhone Ultra. The long-awaited smartphone will be Apple's first foray into the foldable marketplace.

It will be equipped with two screens, with an internal 7.8-inch screen that can be unfolded like a book. A second 5.3-inch display will be on the outside for more typical smartphone usage.

That internal display could be quite unusual for Apple. There are rumors that it could have asymmetrical corners.

A render of what the iPhone Fold could look like - Image Credit: AppleInsider

The model is expected to include premium specifications like the A20 Pro, 12GB of memory, and a large number of cameras. Rumors point to it having a pair of 48-megapixel rear cameras, as well as front-facing 18MP cameras in the front and back screens for video calls.

The lack of a telephoto camera could be a problem for early adopters used to premium specifications.

Rumors say the internal screen's camera could use an under-display system, while the external display will be punch-hole style.

The iPhone Fold also stands to be the most expensive iPhone Apple sells, even ignoring the memory crisis. Pre-issue rumors forecast a price between $2,000 and $2,500, but it could end up being much higher.

Though a launch is anticipated to happen in September, you may not see it in stores until much later. The United States will probably still be the first market it launches in, with a slower rollout elsewhere.

While availability is questionable, the probability of it launching is sky high. On August 23, a report claimed that people have tried out the device ahead of its launch.

Apple Watch

Usually paired with the iPhone launches, you can expect an Apple Watch update too. We aren't expecting much in 2026.

The Apple Watch Series 12 will not benefit from a major overhaul just yet, but it could gain a new health sensor via a fluoroelastomer band and a new band attachment method. Otherwise, don't expect much more than a spec-bump update here.

The Apple Watch Ultra could see an update too, bringing it to version 4. There have been claims of a redesign and new sensors, though rumors have been light on actual detail.

The 2026 update may be a dull one for your wrist, but a revamp is still on the way.

Smart Home

Apple has been working to update its home devices, including the Apple TV and HomePod mini. Both are expected to see updates this fall, after being delayed by the Siri overhaul.

The HomePod mini stands to get a processing upgrade.

In both cases, the expectations are low for overhauls here, with it being more of a functionality-based refresh. Using newer chips for processing, they will be able to support Siri AI.

For the Apple TV 4K, you may also see an update to the Siri Remote, though we're not entirely sure what that will be.

A third smart home device referred to as the Home Hub is also a possibility. An all-new device, it is expected to act as the center of your smart home network, complete with a seven-inch screen and a FaceTime camera.

That screen will manage your smart home devices, display notifications, calendar listings, and other pertinent information, as well as handle communications.

It will take two forms, rumors say, with the first being a half-moon dome with the screen attached to it. A second will attach to mounts using magnets.

While there's no guarantee that all three will make it in September's event, Apple Stores are apparently preparing for some kind of smart home shake-up and brand new devices.

iPad mini 8

While expectations for iPad appearances are low, there is one exception in the form of the iPad mini. The eighth-generation device is anticipated to also have a big glow-up for 2026, thanks to a new display.

The current-gen iPad mini, without OLED.

Rumors and a code leak have indicated that an OLED version is on the way. This should be an 8.4-inch LTPS panel with hybrid OLED, though without ProMotion.

It will also get the usual chip update too, potentially gaining the A20 chip.

AirPods Pro

An accessory often bought alongside the iPhone, AirPods Pro is believed by some to get another update in the latter stages of 2026. While a fairly pedestrian update is a safe bet, there may be something more on the cards.

We have regularly seen rumors about AirPods Pro with cameras to capture the user's environment. Based on a demo video that leaked in a macOS Tahoe beta, they may arrive very soon.

The idea of the cameras is to feed data into Visual Intelligence. A user could then ask questions about what they're looking at or nearby subjects, which Siri can then interpret and respond to.

This may not even need to be a verbal query. Apparently, gesture recognition is a possibility here.

Those cameras will be able to detect people and take stereoscopic imagery, albeit at a low 1-megapixel resolution. But it will still be able to take photos of others on command, complete with an obligatory status light.

Previous rumors said that the camera-equipped version could be out in 2027. The beta leak video hints that it could be here a lot sooner than anyone thought, but the better bet is still for next year.

items.title: iPhone 20 will look like a rounder and thinner iPhone Air
items.content_html:
The iPhone 20 will be a glass-heavy device reminiscent of the iPhone Air but with a more rounded appearance, a Weibo leaker has reiterated.

While we are all waiting for the iPhone 18 to come out of Apple in the very near future, the rumor mill is still infatuated about devices that are still far from launch. With the 20th-anniversary iPhone anticipated in 2027, speculation is rife for what that model will bring.

In a Sunday post to Weibo, leaker Fixed-Focus Digital has called back to a post about the iPhone 10 they made in July. In Sunday's update, the leaker claims about the appearance and thermals of the model.

According to the leaker, the iPhone 20 will use the same glass assembly as the iPhone Air. It won't be a direct copy, as it will instead use more rounded materials, if a machine translation of the post is to be believed.

The leaker doesn't go into detail, but adds that it apparently saved Apple money on the cost of production.

They do go on to add that the heat dissipation and thinness of the model have also been improved. Though, again, they do so without saying how at all.

Rumors repeating themselves

When it comes to Fixed-Focus Digital, they generally have a mixed track record, much like other Weibo-based rumor sources. They have some hits, like the name of the iPhone 16e, but also a lot of misses.

In this particular case, the post doesn't really offer that much new to the overall iPhone 20 picture, aside from a cost saving for Apple. Apple would be fighting for suppliers to make cost-cuts anyway.

The previously mentioned July post from Fixed Focus Digital asserted that Apple had "returned to glass" for the model. Apple was also going to process parts using methods similar to the first-generation Air, too.

In May, another Weibo leaker by the name of Digital Chat Station said Apple had decided to try for a quad-curved OLED display, continuing claims about the screen. Earlier claims again discussed the curvature at length.

The new comment about heat dissipation is also something that Fixed Focus Digital brought up on August 2. At the time, they said the model will have a heat dissipation plate that was an inch larger than in previous models.

In the same post, they added that would be chiefly made from glass and have an iPhone Air-style mid-frame and thinness.

While we at AppleInsider have a duty to report and comment on rumors and speculation for upcoming Apple products, and to judge their accuracy, Weibo leakers don't have the same remit.

It's going to be a year before we see the iPhone 20, and we expect the rumors to improve as that launch gets closer. Here's hoping the Weibo leakers improve too.

items.title: This is the first look at the inside of Apple's AI servers
items.content_html:
Photographs showing the inside of an Apple Silicon AI server have surfaced online, giving a glimpse of how Apple designed its Private Cloud Compute hardware.

Apple's efforts to catch up in the field of AI have already led to the creation of Private Cloud Compute, namely Apple's own brand of secure AI cloud computing.

While it has started to ship its own servers from its facility in Houston, Texas, there hasn't been much coverage about the server hardware itself. While we still don't know about the hardware, we now have a closer look of how it's all laid out internally.

The shots, posted by @hsuchingpo to X on August 24, are listed as being an "Apple M5 Server." When asked by another user if it was Apple Private Cloud Compute, the account responded it was "Most likely" the case.

M5#apple pic.twitter.com/BJE4W0qPWF

— (@hsuchingpo) August 24, 2026

Based on other reporting, we can say with certainty that it is an Apple-produced server.

Four photos are supplied by the account, with the first showing an overhead view of what looks like to be a custom 2U rack-mountable chassis.

Lots of hardware, tiny space

The server has four columns of hardware, with each consisting of eight smaller computer elements. Each board is on the outside edge of the column, with the heatsinks in the middle.

The boards seem to have a main processing chip element in the middle. To the sides are brackets to quickly remove or replace the boards.

Based on eight processors per column, that would mean each server contains 32 of them.

Later shots show those side boards, sans heatsink. A fourth image with the thermal paste cleaned off clearly shows the Apple logo on top of one of the chips.

We can only guess that the chips in use are M5 Ultra-equivalents to maximize performance.

A middle connector bridges the gap in the middle. A main control board runs the full column length, which those smaller boards connect into.

All four of the columns are identical in construction, with one slightly disassembled for the photographs.

In the middle of the unit are connector cables, that lead from the middle of the base board to the center, then to one end of the case. It is unclear if that is for providing power to each column, handling data, or both tasks.

One thing about the server that the account shares is that it's not really in control of what it processes. Another device is used to manage the hardware, which can be the case when creating server clusters.

In this instance, the account says it requires the use of a Mac Studio for "software control."

This may seem a bit unlikely unless the Mac Studio is in another part of the same rack setup. This isn't entirely out of the question, as Mac minis have commonly been rack-mounted for commercial purposes.

Smart cooling

The arrangement is designed to allow as much airflow to pass through the column as efficiently as possible, from front to back. At one end of each column is a single fan, drawing air through.

This is quite a common concept for rack-mounted servers, as they are designed to maximize the use of hardware while keeping them cool enough to work in very confined spaces.

The heatsinks are in the middle of each column, with the fins arranged so air can flow from one end to the other directly. The sides and baseboard are also joined by a clear plastic cover on the top, enclosing the column and forcing air through the passage.

Definitely an Apple server

We have seen that hardware setup before.

Back in February, Apple announced that its Houston facility was producing AI servers ahead of schedule. As part of that launch, it released some promotional shots from inside the facility.

An Apple employee on an AI server production line - Image Credit: Apple

One of those shots gives a side-on view of one of the AI servers, without its top cover. The main plastic-covered section matches the just-surfaced photographs, and it's not hard to imagine the other section being hidden by the cover in the new shots.

The main takeaway of the images is that Apple is clever and meticulous about the insides of its servers.

It may not be on the same level of hardware-stuffing as an iPhone, or a return to the xServe for consumers, but it still puts a lot of thought into what it uses to serve Siri AI queries.

items.title: This iPhone Ultra teaser is almost as good as Apple launch videos
items.content_html:
If this is not how Apple presents the iPhone Ultra, perhaps it should be. A YouTuber has produced a concept video showing how the new device might be used, and launched.

It will probably be September 9, 2026 when John Ternus presents the long-awaited foldable, the iPhone Ultra. He'll do it in a pre-recorded video that will definitely be slick, and definitely persuade you to want to buy.

What it won't be is the new video that is being circulated as a concept. While it does have an on-screen credit for a voiceover by John Ternus, it doesn't even try to mimic his voice.

Whereas it does very well mimic the style of video that Apple has been making since it stopped doing iPhone launches live. In color grading, lighting and general pacing, "Introducing iPhone Ultra" by Gunho Lee is evocative of the first Apple Vision Pro videos.

For a video that is very clear it is not a real Apple ad, this 65-second sequence puts hoaxers to shame. The iPhone Ultra shown in it not only looks perfectly realistic, but the use of it feels natural.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

As an unnamed actor goes through his day, the iPhone Ultra is put through some of its paces. It's taken out of a pocket, it's opened up, and unlocked with Touch ID.

Then it's shown displaying a film, working across two apps, and being used to take a phone call.

There's even a truly Apple-esque moment where the iPhone Ultra floats up out of the actor's hand and we see an exploded view of its insides. This really is a remarkable piece of work with the detailing on the hinge absolutely convincing.

What's a little less convincing, and will probably be better with the real product, is when it's being used open. The wide display is excellent but the actor looks a little awkward trying to balance it while using two apps.

Then one odd thing is that at no point is the front display shown. Given the extraordinary detailing on the hinge shots, it can't be for lack of ability.

It's also not for lack of practice. The same artist recently made a shorter and less detailed "launch video" for the product, although that didn't show the front screen either.

And the same designer has also produced another very different but recognizably Apple-style video for the expected HomePod with a screen.

items.title: M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio: Four years of change, compared
items.content_html:
The M5 Ultra Mac Studio arrives four years after the first, equipped with the M1 Ultra. Here's how the latest top-spec model has moved on from the original big-hitter.

The new Mac Studio appeared with a new M5 Ultra chip on Tuesday, making it the top option for anyone working on AI. It marks the fourth Ultra model to be released, over four years after the very first one was introduced.

Back in March 2022, the M1 Ultra model was viewed as a big deal. Thanks to its processing power, it clearly was.

But three model upgrades and four chip generations later, there's a lot of change to consider when it comes to performance.

Here's how the M5 Ultra Mac Studio measures up against the M1 Ultra version that launched the family in 2022.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio - Specifications

SpecificationsM5 Ultra Mac Studio (2026)M1 Ultra Mac Studio (2022)
Launch starting price$5,499$3,999
Dimensions (inches)7.7 x 7.7 x 3.77.7 x 7.7 x 3.7
Weight (pounds)8.07.9

GraphicsUp to 80-core GPU, third-generation ray tracingUp to 64-core GPU
RAM96GB, 256GB, 512GB64GB, 128GB
Memory bandwidth1.2TB/s800GB/s
NetworkingWi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, 10Gb EthernetWi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.0, 10Gb Ethernet
Storage1TB, 2TB, 4TB, 8TB, 16TB1TB, 2TB, 4TB, 8TB
PortsSix Thunderbolt 5, HDMI, 10Gb Ethernet, Two USB-A, SDXC, 3.5mm headphoneSix Thunderbolt 4, HDMI, 10Gb Ethernet, Two USB-A, SDXC, 3.5mm headphone

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio - Design, Weight, Size

Apple has left the Mac Studio exterior untouched across four years and multiple chips. The compact round-cornered aluminum block of the current edition measures 7.7 inches square and 3.7 inches tall, identical to the 2022 model.

Likewise, there's not much difference when weight is involved. The M1 Ultra is lighter at 7.9 pounds, but the M5 Ultra's extra mass at 8 pounds won't be noticed on your desktop, and probably not when you pick it up either.

The front has stayed consistent, with a pair of Thunderbolt 4 ports for M1 Ultra or Thunderbolt 5 for M5 Ultra alongside a memory card reader. The only thing that's changed here is the standard those ports run on, as the appearance is certainly identical between generations.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio: A Mac Studio at home on a desk.

Turning to the back reveals the usual row of ports, along with the large grille section that dominates the rear. That grille is, again, the same size and design in both models.

The raised circular base with vent holes is also unchanged, complete with the same vent holes for cooling. All of your mounts and so forth you have for the M1 Ultra are still usable for the M5 Ultra model.

Obviously, Apple tends to reuse a design that works for multiple iterations. That certainly seems to be the case for the Mac Studio.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio - Processor and graphics

Beyond AI, which we will get to, the performance gulf here is enormous. Four years and four generations of Apple Silicon separate these two chips.

The M5 Ultra starts with a 30-core CPU, using 10 super cores and 20 performance cores. You can scale this up to 36 cores, with 12 super cores and 24 performance cores.

The M1 Ultra, by contrast, used a 20-core CPU with 16 performance cores and 4 efficiency cores. There was only one CPU configuration, so the M5 Ultra offers far more cores at either tier.

In both cases, Apple combines equivalent Max chips using a high-speed interconnect known as UltraFusion. For the M5 Ultra, Apple joins two dual-die M5 Max chips for a quad-die architecture, a first for the company.

Mac Studio M5 Ultra

The M5 Ultra Mac Studio can be configured with up to a 36-core CPU and up to an 80-core GPU.
Buy at Adorama
Buy at B&H
Buy at Expercom

The result is an inter-die bandwidth of a staggering 4.4TB/s. The M1 Ultra's original UltraFusion managed 2.5TB/s, itself still impressive.

On graphics, the M1 Ultra shipped with a 48-core or 64-core GPU, with no hardware ray tracing at all. The M5 Ultra uses a 64-core or 80-core GPU, with added hardware-accelerated ray tracing.

Ray tracing brings more realistic lighting, shadows, and reflections to 3D and design work. It is a capability the M1 Ultra could do, but not with the ease of the hardware-accelerated assistance the M5 Ultra's GPU has.

Apple puts a figure on the rendering gain too. It cites up to 4.7 times faster scene rendering in Maxon Redshift on the M5 Ultra than the M1 Ultra.

This is a large jump where 3D and visual effects artists are concerned.

There are Media Engines at play for both models, for hardware-accelerated video encoding and decoding. The M1 Ultra handled H.264, HEVC, ProRes, and ProRes RAW, with two video decode engines and four video encode engines, as well as four ProRes encode and decode engines.

The M5 Ultra doesn't really break this pattern too much. Though it does have AV1 decode capabilities.

On memory, the two are a generation apart in capacity. The M1 Ultra had 64GB or 128GB configurations, while the M5 Ultra scales from 96GB to 256GB, and up to 512GB if you could afford it.

There is also a large gap in memory bandwidth. The M5 Ultra moves data at 1.2 terabytes per second, half as fast again as the M1 Ultra's 800 gigabytes per second.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio - The bigger AI push

The Mac Studio was always pushed as the performance model by Apple. But for the M5 generation, it's framed around accelerating on-device artificial intelligence.

The key change is the GPU. For the first time, the Ultra chip tier gains Neural Accelerators embedded in each graphics core, purpose-built for the matrix math that drives AI models.

Both models still include a Neural Engine, a 32-core version in each case that doubles the cores of other non-Ultra chips. But the M1 Ultra's Neural Engine works alone, without the great GPU acceleration the M5 Ultra now brings.

Pairing a 32-core Neural Engine with up to 80 GPU cores full of Neural Accelerators gives the M5 Ultra a combination the M1 Ultra could not approach.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio: You can't really tell the difference between the generations, from the outside.

Apple claims the M5 Ultra has up to 9.8 times the peak AI compute of the M1 Ultra as a result. That is a vast leap that AI researchers simply cannot ignore.

It quotes the M5 Ultra Mac Studio as being up to 9.8 times faster at large language model prompt processing in LM Studio than the M1 Ultra, and up to 8.2 times faster at text-to-image generation.

Machine learning training shows the widest gap of all. Apple cites up to 15.4 times faster CopyCat ML training in Foundry Nuke on the M5 Ultra compared to the M1 Ultra.

The payoff is the ability to run enormous language models entirely on the machine. Apple frames this as freedom from cloud costs and token limits, with the added privacy of keeping data local.

For an M1 Ultra owner working in AI, that gap is the single most compelling reason to look at the new model. The older machine was never designed with local large language models in mind, but Apple adapted to the market with the 2026 refresh.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio - Benchmarks

The M5 Ultra is not available for anyone to perform benchmarks on it just yet. But that said, we can pull out some data points based on Apple's claims and another product to have an idea of what to expect.

The most accurate thing we could possibly determine independently of Apple's PR is single-core performance in Geekbench 7.

Since the single-core test relies on the processor using the fastest core available, we can turn to the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5. The Super Cores in it will be the same as in the M5 Ultra, only fewer in number.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio: Single-core

The M5 in the MacBook Pro can score 3,637 on the single-core test. Geekbench's results browser shows the M1 Ultra hitting 2,225 for the same test.

The result indicates the M5 Ultra will be noticeably faster than the single-core performance of the M1 Ultra. It's close to double the performance.

While we can be pretty certain about the single-core speeds, we will have to estimate for multi-core and Metal. This means extrapolating from Apple's claims.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio: Multi-core

For multi-core, Apple says the M5 Ultra delivers up to 1.3 times higher multithreaded performance than the M3 Ultra. We previously determined that to be a score around 50,000.

The M1 Ultra Mac Studio, on the other hand, hits 23,357 in Geekbench's listings. This is a respectable score, but the estimate shows there's been a considerable boost over the years.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio: Metal

For Metal, Apple said the M5 Ultra has 40% faster graphics performance than the M3 Ultra. Based on a Geekbench score of 244,854 for the M3 Ultra Mac Studio, that would turn into something in the region of 350,000 for the M5 Ultra Mac Studio.

The listing for the M1 Ultra Mac Studio on Geekbench doesn't say how many GPU cores it has, but the 153,805 score is probably for the upper-tier 64-core GPU.

Regardless, there is a massive gulf when it comes to graphical performance.

We'll update all of these charts when actual benchmarks are available.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio - Ports and Connectivity

Despite visual similarities, the physical ports have moved on more than they first appear. The M5 Ultra offers six Thunderbolt 5 ports, with two at the front and four at the back.

The M1 Ultra also had six Thunderbolt ports in the same layout, but they were the slower Thunderbolt 4 standard. Thunderbolt 5 pushes the available bandwidth to 120Gbps in some situations, a real gain for displays and docks.

That said, 40Gbps in Thunderbolt 4 isn't too shabby.

Both share HDMI, a 10Gb Ethernet connection, a pair of USB 3 Type-A ports, and a headphone jack that supports high-impedance headphones. Thunderbolt aside, the rear selection is otherwise very familiar.

On the wireless side, the leap is larger.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio: The rear ports haven't changed much, aside from the Thunderbolt generation.

The M1 Ultra used Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.0, which was more than serviceable for the time. Both then and now, if you need fast network access, you'd go for the 10Gb Ethernet connection.

The M5 Ultra moves to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, thanks to a switch to Apple's N1 chip.

That N1 chip also adds Thread networking, which the M1 Ultra never offered. For a smart-home hub or modern wireless setup, the M5 Ultra is far better equipped.

That said, someone who owns a Mac Studio probably has a HomePod mini or an Apple TV 4K for smart home management.

Display support has grown too. The M1 Ultra drove up to five displays, consisting of four 6K 60Hz screens and one 4K 60Hz on HDMI.

Now, the M5 Ultra handles up to eight, meaning up to eight 6K screens at 60Hz, or up to four 8K screens at 60Hz. Or even four 4K screens at 240Hz.

This is an area that's more to do with professional signage and sets for performances, rather than home users. Then again, we are in a device budget range where someone could make an overkill display arrangement at home.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio - Storage and clustering

Storage sees a genuine architectural upgrade. The M5 Ultra uses a next-generation SSD built on PCIe Gen 6, which Apple says doubles storage speed over the previous Mac Studio generation.

That matters a lot when you're loading large AI models or shifting uncompressed footage around. Faster storage means less of a wait for things to load, after all.

This time around, Apple is leaning into clustering as part of its AI talking points. Using Thunderbolt 5 and remote direct memory access, several modern Macs can pool their memory into one shared resource.

Apple says a cluster of four Mac Studio systems delivers up to three times the AI inference performance of a single machine.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio: Clustering is always an option, but it's better on M5

The M1 Ultra had no equivalent clustering story, as the concept was not part of its pitch in 2022. This didn't mean you couldn't do it.

Tools such as Exo and MLX allowed earlier Macs to talk to each other and pool their memory and computer power over Thunderbolt or Ethernet.

You definitely could cluster with an M1 Ultra Mac Studio and other devices. You won't, however, get the same bandwidth and other improvements Apple has introduced to MLX, let alone the AI benefits of those GPU neural accelerators.

For storage capacity, the M5 Ultra also stretches further.

Both start at 1TB and double through the range. The M1 Ultra topped out at 8TB, while the M5 Ultra adds a 16TB tier above that.

However, the few people who go for that top tier of storage will pay a considerable sum to do so, thanks to the memory crisis and Apple's premium upgrade charges.

It's more probable that a corporate buyer will opt for less storage and instead rely on external or network storage devices than pay the high prices.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio - Price

The M5 Ultra Mac Studio starts at $5,499, with education pricing at $5,099. That is well above the M1 Ultra's $3,999 starting point from 2022.

The original M1 Ultra base included the 20-core CPU, 48-core GPU, 64GB of memory, and 1TB of storage. An upgrade to the 64-core GPU cost $1,000 more, while 128GB of memory was another $800.

Storage upgrades were $400 more to go from 2TB, another $600 again from 2TB to 4TB, and $2,200 on top of that to go from 4TB to 8TB.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio: The front ports and memory card reader. The former is better on M5, the latter's not changed.

Much has changed in the years since, including the current memory market. High-capacity memory upgrades on the M5 Ultra are far more expensive than anything Apple charged for the M1 Ultra.

Going from 96GB to 256GB on the M5 Ultra costs a steep $4,000. The 512GB memory option is not available until October, and is expected to cost considerably more.

Storage upgrades have also climbed. Going from the base 1TB to 2TB is an extra $500. Getting 4TB is $1,500. Going to 4TB to 8TB costs $3500.

If you want the upgrade to 16TB of storage, that's $7500 on its own. At this point, you should consider external Thunderbolt 5 SSD storage which will be very close to as fast as the internal drive for about 60% of the cost.

The Mac Studio has always been expensive, and so have its upgrades. It's just worse right now, and will be for a few years, at least.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio vs M1 Ultra Mac Studio - Which to buy

It's not hard to believe the M5 Ultra Mac Studio has leapt forward in performance since the line came out. Four years of progress and a multi-generational technology jump will make sure of that.

This is not intended as a word processing machine, that's what the Mac mini and iMac are for. This is for heavy lifting, deep, long processing runs. And like Apple says, AI loads.

It's far enough of a jump that the M1 Ultra Mac Studio owner has a very good case to pick up the M5 Ultra version. There's more than a sufficient amount of improvement to justify such a move.

That said, it's also safe to say that Apple's expected customer for the Mac Studio has also changed over the years.

The M1 Ultra arrived as something that can seriously crunch the numbers of any task. It was a creative professional's dream machine. It still is for many, and will remains so for some time.

Apple is pitching the M5 Ultra at a slightly different crowd now. Sure, the performance is there, but the massive potential for machine learning tasks and AI training means the intended audience has shifted considerably.

On the design side of things, Thunderbolt 5 is nice, and improved amounts of storage and monitor connectivity help too, but there's not much externally that's really changed.

To be fair, for the Mac Studio, it's never been about the looks. It's always about the massive processing potential inside that aluminum casing.

The honest summary is simple. If your work is creative and the M1 Ultra still keeps up, there is no rush to upgrade.

But if AI, other other heavy processing lift is central to what you do, the M5 Ultra is a generational leap worth taking.

When we review this machine, we'll be discussing it in context with the actual workflows that we've been using for the last few years, and how much faster they've gotten. We're looking forward to that.

And, if you're coming from a M1 Ultra Mac Studio, and aren't looking at heavy AI lifting, the M5 Max Mac Studio outperforms it in every regard. More on that in a while.

Where to buy Apple's M5 Ultra Mac Studio and M1 Ultra Mac Studio

Apple's M5 Ultra Mac Studio can be ordered now at B&H Photo and Adorama, with prices starting at $5,499. Our M5 Ultra Mac Studio Price Guide provides easy price comparison across popular Apple resellers.

Deals on open-box and pre-owned M1 Ultra Mac Studio configurations can be found on eBay, with prices as low as $2,134.95 at press time.

items.title: Apple's viral iPhone Ultra tease has probably been lost in translation
items.content_html:
It's fun to look at Apple invite graphics, and speculate, but it can go off the rails. Apple fans are arguing semantics over whether a Chinese event tagline contains a cheeky nod to the iPhone Ultra.

It's not a big secret that the folding iPhone is likely in about two weeks. Let's not read too much into what Google Translate says, though.

If you visit the China Mainland Apple homepage in Chrome, and then translate the text to English, you're greeted with the tagline "A new chapter unfolds, let's shine!"

Some people believe that Apple has done this as a cheeky way to hint that it's about to unveil its first foldable phone, the iPhone Ultra.

Other people point out that Chrome's in-page translation feature is the only one that adds the word "unfold." We've looked, and spoken to native speakers.

The single translation failure seems to be true. When prodded, Google Translate changes the text to "unveil a new chapter and shine bright."

It's even sparked a minor debate on X over whether or not this is a good or bad translation.

There seems to be a misconception going around right now about the Apple Event invite text in China

Google's in-page translation service claims it says "a new chapter unfolds"

All other translation services, AIs, and even Chinese speakers are saying this is a poor translation.

— Aaron (@aaronp613) August 26, 2026

For its part, Safari translates it as "Bright new chapter, come to dazzling."

All of these seem to be more in line with Apple's English tagline, "Surprise and shine."

But you can't really blame people for reading into the translation. And far be it from me to deny people the pleasure of arguing semantics. I love arguing semantics.

After all, Apple is inherently cheeky with its event taglines. I wouldn't put it past it to be cryptically punny. In fact, it often is.

In October 2023, Apple used "Scary Fast," which was both a Halloween pun and hinted at the M3 chip lineup.

In September 2022, Apple's tagline was "Far Out." That was the year that Apple introduced the Emergency SOS via satellite feature and the Apple Watch Ultra.

And in 2020, it used "Hi, Speed" and introduced the first 5G-enabled iPhone.

So there is precedent here.

Lost in translation

To be clear, I don't think Google, or Chrome specifically, was trying to drop some sort of hint or infer Apple's intention, either. I think this was just a machine translation attempting to make Chinese wordplay make sense to English speakers.

Trying to directly translate nearly anything from one language to another without human nuance is an exercise in futility. A lot of translation requires at least a bit of knowledge of both cultures and the willingness to do a bit of creative bridging between the two.

A Chinese pun, when directly translated, won't necessarily make sense to someone who grew up speaking English. After all, "Surprise and Shine," when directly translated to Chinese, doesn't read as a "rise and shine" pun, either.

Of course, the Chinese Xin pian does mean "new chapter," and Apple's first foldable will open like a book. And Apple Taiwan's page, which displays text in traditional Chinese, says that a new chapter will open.

Again, it could be nothing, but it would be silly to assume that Apple isn't spending considerable time and effort crafting cheeky taglines in all its supported languages, either.

items.title: Built-in Genlock makes the Mac Studio a boon for professional video production
items.content_html:
Apple has added Genlock to the new Mac Studio and the M5 Pro Mac mini. If you already know what that does for you, you've already called your production manager to make a purchase.

It wasn't the most high-profile aspect of the newly updated Mac Studio, but Genlock will be the reason some users buy it. Genlock is a system for synchronizing footage from multiple cameras and saves potentially hours of manually aligning video and audio tracks.

Genlock has been used by broadcast television productions for decades, and it has been supported by Macs and PCs before. However, it required third-party external hardware that was expensive and complex to use.

For filmmakers and streamers

Apple added Genlock support to the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max back in 2025. Describing it as one of filmmakers' most requested features, senior vice president of worldwide marketing, Greg Joswiak, said it was particularly for content creators and streamers.

"Whether using multiple cameras or onscreen graphics, Genlock allows for accurate and professional-looking transitions without hours of manual frame-by-frame alignment," he said.

"When using an array of cameras, Genlock enables advanced filmmaking tools and techniques like time-splicing, or 'bullet time,'" he continued, "which allows filmakers to change the audience's perspective while freezing time."

The iPhone 17 Pro models supported Genlock via a then-new Blackmagic Design Camera ProDoc. Apple updated Final Cut Camera to utilize this and shoot video that was genlocked and streamed live to iPads.

Adding Genlock to the Mac

Apple also provided Genlock APIs for other firms, but the biggest move has been adding it as standard to the new M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studio models, plus the New Mac mini. Apple has not given Macs the ability to take footage directly from Final Cut Camera, but it has improved the handling of Genlocked footage.

Genlocking multiple cameras means you can freeze one single moment and show it from many angles - image credit: Apple.

Joswiak is right that the most obvious and very, very welcome improvement is that the footage from multiple cameras is already aligned when it's ingested into Final Cut Pro or other video editing apps.

But beyond that convenience, Genlock also keeps audio in sync. It's common to select one audio source to be heard regardless of which video is being shown, but if you are switching microphones, Genlock should mean it just works.

Then at the same time, in every sense of that phrase, Genlock improves playback in editing sessions. It's most noticeable with a separate external or reference monitor where without Genlock, it's possible to get dropped frames or other issues.

Mac Studio on location

The fact that you can't feed video live from the Final Cut Camera app on iPhone to the Mac Studio is a limitation. It means productions will either still use iPads for monitoring and control during the shoot, or not ingest the footage until later.

Macs can be used in live broadcast production, though. And the addition of Genlock to the Mac Studio will improve switching between camera feeds. It's intended to prevent distractions for the viewer such as digital artefacts remaining on screen, or simply for timings to not feel right.

Apple has not stated whether it used Genlock in May 2026 when it filmed an entire LA Galaxy and Houston Dynamo FC match solely using iPhones. But that recording was using more than a dozen iPhone 17 Pro models with live switching so it probably did.

Yet as impressive a feat as that was in so many ways, viewers still noticed visible compression, heavy image processing, and even shaky tracking shots.

So Genlock is only part of a professional video shoot, but it can be a key one. And now having it supported natively in the Mac Studio does mean that more new Mac Studios with Thunderbolt 5 will making their way into edit suites.

items.title: Apple's new & cheaper Apple Polishing Cloth almost as good as the original
items.content_html:
I tested out Apple's updated polishing cloth. It still cleans fine, and there are still cheaper options.

The Apple Polishing Cloth first arrived on the scene in 2021 with a $19 price tag. It's easily mocked as it is just a fancy cleaning cloth.

Its popularity was unrivaled, but it's uncertain how many were bought outside of video producers, honestly.

In the early days, Apple Polishing Cloth was routinely out of stock, both in stores and online. Over time, Apple's made it a regular practice to update the cloth's compatibility with new product releases.

It's one of six cleaning cloths that Apple has released in recent years, believe it or not.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

Now the cloth itself has been updated. Sort of.

From bottom to top: Apple Vision Pro cloth, Studio Display cloth, MacBook Pro cloth, original Apple Polishing Cloth, new Apple Polishing Cloth

All slightly different, there is a polishing cloth for Apple Vision Pro, one for the iPad Pro with nano-texture finish, one for the Pro Display XDR, one for the Studio Display with nano-texture finish, the original Apple Polishing Cloth, and second-generation Apple Polishing Cloth.

Out with the old, in with the new

Apple's freshly-revamped cleaning cloth hasn't changed much. It's still a 6.3-inch by 6.3-inch square of material with rounded corners.

Unboxing the Apple Polishing Cloth

It's a dual-layer cloth with edges that are fused together. An Apple logo is stamped onto the lower-right corner of both cloths.

From bottom to top: Apple Vision Pro cloth, Studio Display cloth, MacBook Pro cloth, original Apple Polishing Cloth, new Apple Polishing Cloth

Comparing the two, the new version is using a different material than its predecessor. The original felt almost suede-like while the new one looks like more of a standard microfiber.

The new material, that Apple calls simply a "soft, nonabrasive material," is quite a bit softer and less stiff. Since it's still a dual-layer cloth, this makes it easier to hold as you're cleaning.

The Apple Vision Pro cloth (left), the new Apple Polishing Cloth (center), and the old Apple Polishing Cloth (right)

At the same time, the thinner material feels cheaper than the original, and I don't mean cost. It's more akin to the large and thin polishing cloth included with the Apple Vision Pro, but with a two-layer construction than it was to the first official Apple Polishing Cloth.

No more fingerprints

The Apple Polishing Cloth is very soft and protective. Apple says that it is specifically designed for all of its display finishes, including nano-texture which can be damaged by poor-quality fabrics.

Apple Polishing Cloth Looks very nice with a light grey color

With a change in material and price, I wanted to know how well the cloth would clean. Even though it was $20 for a cleaning cloth, the first one was basically the best-performing cleaning cloth I'd used. Opinions vary amongst the staff here.

Before and after using the new Apple Polishing Cloth

When taking photos or shooting video, I have to clean product displays often. Using the old Apple Polishing Cloth was a daily task.

Fortunately, it seems just as good as before. It doesn't feel like it grabs oils as well, but the results were the same in the end.

The new Apple Polishing Cloth is more flexible

Before, I thought it was the best cleaning cloth around. Now, I think it's a little more average, but still very effective.

Grab your own

If you want a very good cleaning cloth for all your devices, the new Apple Polishing Cloth is a solid choice.

Apple Polishing Cloth is the same size as before

You can buy both in-store and online from Apple for $9. If you want a cloth comparable to the original, the Cloth Pro Max from Copland Supply has been the closest match I've found.

Or, you could get five of them more similar to the original without the Apple stamp, for $7.79, delivered. Your choice.
